Crowdsourcing quality control relies on manual post-hoc checks; no inter-annotator agreement (IAA) metrics reported
8.7% corpus loss during verification step; impact on final dataset representativeness and potential bias not discussed
Suitability for micro-planning is inferred from dataset properties, not directly validated through task-specific evaluation
No comparison with alternative content selection methods (e.g., random sampling, rule-based selection) to validate ILP approach

identified_claims.claim_label: DBPNLG exhibits greater linguistic diversity than RNNLG
identified_claims.claim_text: The resulting DBPNLG dataset, though smaller than Wen et al. (2016)'s RNNLG dataset, exhibits significantly greater linguistic and semantic diversity across multiple dimensions: more attributes (172 vs 108), more input patterns (58 distinct shapes vs 6), lower input-pattern repetition ratio (2.40 vs 10.31), and deeper input trees (depth up to 5 vs depth 1).
evidence: Table 3 reports: DBPNLG 172 attributes vs RNNLG 108; DBPNLG 58 input shapes vs RNNLG 6
Table 3 reports: DBPNLG input/pattern ratio 2.40 vs RNNLG 10.31
Section 4.1 states RNNLG inputs are trees of depth 1; DBPNLG inputs have depth up to 5 with 49.6% of inputs having depth > 1
Examples 3 and 4 illustrate how different attributes induce different syntactic realisations
uncertainty_flags: Attribute count comparison assumes direct semantic equivalence between RNNLG dialog-act attributes and DBpedia RDF properties; no validation of comparability
Input shape diversity measured by count of distinct shapes; no analysis of whether all 58 shapes are linguistically meaningful or some are rare artifacts with minimal impact
Claim that deeper trees 'favour' certain syntactic constructs (Section 3, Figure 1) is intuitive but not empirically validated on the actual datasets; correlation not quantified
No statistical significance testing reported for differences in attribute counts, shape diversity, or repetition ratios
Diversity ≠ complexity: more attributes and shapes may not necessarily make the generation task harder; depends on model architecture and learning dynamics

identified_claims.claim_label: DBPNLG texts are more complex and linguistically sophisticated
identified_claims.claim_text: DBPNLG texts are more complex and linguistically sophisticated: longer (more tokens and sentences per text), higher lexical diversity (CTTR), higher lexical sophistication (LS), and larger vocabulary relative to corpus size.
evidence: Table 4 reports: DBPNLG 18.2 tokens/text vs RNNLG 16.8; DBPNLG 1.47 sentences/text vs RNNLG 1.23
Table 4 reports: DBPNLG CTTR 0.0649 vs RNNLG 0.0589; DBPNLG LS 0.1847 vs RNNLG 0.1523
Table 4 reports: DBPNLG 2992 types / 290479 tokens vs RNNLG 3524 types / 531871 tokens (proportionally higher vocabulary in DBPNLG)
Examples 5 and 6 illustrate text length and complexity differences
uncertainty_flags: Text length differences are modest (18.2 vs 16.8 tokens ≈ 8% difference; 1.47 vs 1.23 sentences ≈ 20% difference); statistical significance not reported; confidence intervals missing
CTTR and LS computed using external tool (Lu 2012); no validation that these metrics are appropriate or meaningful for data-to-text corpora; no correlation with generation difficulty demonstrated

Vocabulary comparison conflates absolute size (RNNLG has more types: 3524 vs 2992) with relative size (DBPNLG has higher type/token ratio); interpretation depends on learning objective and model capacity
Higher LS may reflect rare entity names (proper nouns) rather than linguistic sophistication; no analysis of LS distribution or breakdown by word class
No analysis of whether text complexity differences are due to dataset properties or crowdsourcing procedure (e.g., merging single-triple verbalisations may artificially increase length)

identified_claims.claim_label: Increased complexity validated by lower seq2seq performance
identified_claims.claim_text: The increased complexity of DBPNLG is empirically validated by lower sequence-to-sequence model performance (higher perplexity and lower BLEU), indicating a more challenging learning task that better exercises micro-planning subtasks (lexicalisation, aggregation, surface realisation, sentence segmentation, referring expression generation).
evidence: Table 5 reports: DBPNLG perplexity 8.47 (full delexicalisation) vs RNNLG 6.89; DBPNLG 7.21 (name-only) vs RNNLG 5.89
Table 5 reports: DBPNLG BLEU 0.3891 vs RNNLG 0.4582 (full delexicalisation); DBPNLG 0.4156 vs RNNLG 0.5123 (name-only)
Section 4.3 uses Vinyals et al. (2015) seq2seq model with attention; balanced sample of 13K pairs used for fair comparison
Section 5 concludes: 'data-to-text corpora built by our framework are challenging for such models'
uncertainty_flags: Causal claim (complexity → lower performance) assumes lower performance is solely due to dataset properties, not model architecture, hyperparameter choices, or training dynamics
Balanced sampling (13K pairs) reduces RNNLG from full size; comparison is not on original datasets at their natural scales; RNNLG may benefit from larger training set
Perplexity and BLEU are indirect proxies for 'exercising micro-planning subtasks'; no direct evaluation of whether models actually learn lexicalisation, aggregation, etc.
No error analysis provided; unclear whether lower performance reflects genuine complexity or dataset-specific phenomena (e.g., rare vocabulary, unusual structures, delexicalisation artifacts)
Hyperparameters (3 layers, 512 units) not tuned per dataset; may be suboptimal for one or both datasets
No comparison with other model architectures (e.g., structured models, hierarchical models, copy mechanisms) that might handle complexity differently
BLEU scores are low for both datasets (0.39–0.51); unclear whether differences are meaningful or both models are struggling

identified_claims.claim_label: RDF-based content selection produces varied and coherent data units
identified_claims.claim_text: RDF-based content selection using bigram coherence models (sibling, chain, and mixed) produces more varied and coherent data units than enumeration of dialog acts and attribute combinations.
evidence: Section 3.2 describes three bigram models (S-Model for siblings, C-Model for chains, M-Model for mixed) learned from category graphs
Section 3.2 formulates content selection as ILP to select subtrees with maximal bigram probability
Table 1 shows results across 6 categories and 3 bigram models with varying triple counts (1–7)
Section 3 contrasts this with Wen et al. (2016)'s enumeration approach
uncertainty_flags: No direct comparison of coherence between ILP-selected units and enumerated units; 'coherence' is assumed to follow from bigram probability but not validated on actual selected units
Bigram models trained on category graphs; unclear how well these capture coherence for out-of-category entities, cross-category relations, or entities with atypical property distributions
Table 1 reports counts of inputs and patterns but does not evaluate coherence, relevance, or semantic adequacy of selected units; no human evaluation of coherence
ILP formulation details incomplete: objective function, constraints, solver parameters, and convergence criteria not fully specified; reproducibility compromised
No ablation study comparing S-Model, C-Model, and M-Model; unclear which model(s) contribute most to diversity and coherence
Variety measured by count of inputs and patterns; no analysis of whether variety translates to linguistic diversity in generated text

identified_claims.claim_label: Framework applicable to other RDF knowledge bases
identified_claims.claim_text: The framework can be used to create a data-to-text corpus from any knowledge base where entities are categorised and there is a large number of entities belonging to the same category, and could be applied to e.g., MusicBrainz, FOAF or LinkedGeoData.
evidence: Section 3 states: 'it can be used to create a data-to-text corpus from any knowledge base where entities are categorised and there is a large number of entities belonging to the same category'
Section 5 mentions 'many large scale datasets are encoded in the RDF language (e.g., MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData)'
Section 3 notes the framework is 'generic' and applicable beyond DBpedia
uncertainty_flags: Generalizability claim is theoretical; framework tested only on DBpedia with 6 categories (out of 14 collected but not yet processed)
Applicability to other RDF KBs depends on availability of category hierarchies, sufficient entity density, and property distributions similar to DBpedia; not all RDF KBs have these properties
Crowdsourcing procedure includes manual property clarification step (Section 3.3); effort and cost required for other KBs not estimated; may not scale
No evidence that bigram coherence models trained on one KB transfer to another; models may be KB-specific
No discussion of how framework handles KBs with different schema complexity, property types, or entity distributions
Claim about applicability to MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData is speculative; no pilot study or feasibility analysis provided

strengths.title: Novel framework combining ILP and crowdsourcing for corpus generation
strengths.description: The semi-automatic approach is well-motivated and addresses real limitations of existing methods. ILP-based content selection from RDF graphs is a principled way to generate varied, coherent data units, and crowdsourcing ensures data-text alignment. The combination is creative and represents a meaningful methodological contribution.
evidence: Section 3 clearly articulates limitations of existing approaches (domain-specific corpora, expert-annotated corpora, enumeration-based crowdsourcing)
Framework design rationale is well-explained: ILP for coherence, crowdsourcing for alignment, RDF for real KB data
Example 1 demonstrates the approach produces realistic, complex data-text pairs

strengths.title: Comprehensive comparative analysis with multiple metrics
strengths.description: The paper provides a thorough comparison of DBPNLG and RNNLG across multiple dimensions: dataset size, attribute diversity, input shape distribution, text complexity, and neural model performance. This multi-faceted evaluation is more informative than single-metric comparisons.
evidence: Table 3 compares 5 dataset properties (attributes, inputs, patterns, entities, input/pattern ratio, input shapes)
Table 4 compares 6 text properties (tokens, sentences, vocabulary, CTTR, LS, TTR)
Table 5 provides seq2seq performance on both datasets in two delexicalisation modes
Section 4 systematically addresses each dimension with examples and interpretation

strengths.title: Clear motivation for micro-planning support through input diversity
strengths.description: The paper articulates a plausible connection between input structure (depth, shape, attribute combinations) and the micro-planning subtasks (lexicalisation, aggregation, surface realisation, sentence segmentation, referring expression generation). Figure 1 and Examples 3–4 effectively illustrate this connection.
evidence: Figure 1 shows how path vs. branching structures favour different syntactic constructs
Examples 3 and 4 demonstrate how attribute combinations induce different syntactic realisations
Section 3 explains why deeper trees and more attributes support learning of complex generation operations

strengths.title: Rigorous crowdsourcing quality control procedure
strengths.description: The four-step crowdsourcing procedure (property clarification, single-triple verbalisations, multi-triple merging, quality verification) is well-designed to minimize errors and ensure semantic adequacy. Automatic validators, manual checks, and majority-vote verification provide multiple layers of quality assurance.
evidence: Section 3.3 describes 12 custom JavaScript validators to prevent spamming and invalid input
Manual post-hoc checks eliminate mismatched pairs
5-answer majority vote on fluency, semantic adequacy, and grammaticality
8.7% corpus loss indicates quality threshold is enforced

strengths.title: Practical resource contribution with planned release
strengths.description: The paper commits to releasing DBPNLG as part of a shared task, which will benefit the NLG community. The dataset is designed to support training of KB verbalisers and micro-planners, addressing a real need in the field.
evidence: Section 5 states: 'we will make it available as part of a shared task for evaluating data-to-text micro-planners'
Dataset is uploaded with submission
Framework is applicable to other RDF KBs, enabling future corpus creation

strengths.title: Honest acknowledgment of limitations and future work
strengths.description: The paper acknowledges that only 6 out of 14 collected categories have been processed, that seq2seq models may not be optimal for complex texts, and that further work is needed. This transparency is commendable.
evidence: Section 5: 'While we only report on a dataset developed using 6 DBpedia categories, we have collected content for 14 further categories'
Section 5: 'sequence-to-sequence models have been proposed for generation. Our experiments suggest that these are not optimal when it comes to generate linguistically complex texts'

concerns.title: Unvalidated assumption: bigram probability as proxy for coherence
concerns.description: The paper assumes that maximizing bigram probability over RDF properties produces coherent and relevant data units, but provides no direct validation of this assumption. Bigram probability is a statistical measure that may not capture semantic coherence or pragmatic relevance.
evidence: Section 3.2 states: 'sibling and chain models capture different types of coherence, namely, topic-based coherence for the S-Model and discourse-based coherence for the C-Model' (intuitive but not empirically validated)
Table 1 reports counts of inputs and patterns but does not evaluate coherence of selected units
No human evaluation of coherence or relevance of ILP-selected data units
No comparison with alternative content selection methods (e.g., random sampling, rule-based selection)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct human evaluation of coherence and relevance for a sample of ILP-selected data units (e.g., 50–100 units). Compare with random sampling or rule-based baselines. Report inter-annotator agreement and coherence scores.

concerns.title: Missing inter-annotator agreement metrics for crowdsourcing quality
concerns.description: The paper reports crowdsourcing quality control procedures but does not provide inter-annotator agreement (IAA) metrics (e.g., Cohen's kappa, Fleiss' kappa) for the majority-vote validation step. IAA is a standard metric for assessing annotation quality and reliability.
evidence: Section 3.3, Step 4 describes 5-answer majority vote but does not report IAA
No breakdown of agreement rates by category or by criterion (fluency, semantic adequacy, grammaticality)
8.7% corpus loss is reported but no analysis of which types of pairs were rejected or why
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute and report Cohen's kappa or Fleiss' kappa for the majority-vote validation step. Provide breakdown by category and by criterion. Analyze rejected pairs to identify common error patterns.

concerns.title: Incomplete ILP formulation specification
concerns.description: The paper describes the ILP formulation for content selection but does not provide complete technical details: objective function, constraints, solver parameters, convergence criteria, and computational complexity. This limits reproducibility and makes it difficult to assess the method's robustness.
evidence: Section 3.2 states: 'the content selection task is formulated as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem to select, for a given entity of category C and its entity graph Ge, subtrees of Ge with maximal bigram probability and varying size (between 1 and 7 RDF triples)' but does not provide formal specification
No details on ILP solver used, solver parameters, or convergence criteria
No analysis of computational complexity or scalability
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide formal ILP specification: objective function, constraints, variable definitions. Specify solver used and parameters. Provide pseudocode or algorithm description. Discuss computational complexity and scalability.

concerns.title: Causal claim about complexity not adequately supported
concerns.description: The paper claims that lower seq2seq performance on DBPNLG indicates greater complexity, but this is a correlational finding, not causal. Lower performance could result from model architecture, hyperparameter choices, training dynamics, or dataset-specific phenomena (e.g., rare vocabulary, delexicalisation artifacts) rather than inherent complexity.
evidence: Section 4.3 and Table 5 show lower perplexity and BLEU for DBPNLG but do not rule out alternative explanations
No error analysis provided; unclear whether errors reflect complexity or other factors
Hyperparameters (3 layers, 512 units) not tuned per dataset; may be suboptimal for one or both
No comparison with other model architectures that might handle complexity differently
Balanced sampling (13K pairs) may disadvantage RNNLG if it benefits from larger training set
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct error analysis on seq2seq outputs for both datasets. Categorize errors (e.g., missing content, hallucinated content, grammatical errors, rare vocabulary). Compare error distributions. Tune hyperparameters per dataset or use architecture-agnostic complexity metrics (e.g., input entropy, output entropy).

concerns.title: Metric appropriateness not validated for data-to-text corpora
concerns.description: The paper uses CTTR, LS, and TTR to measure text complexity and linguistic sophistication, but these metrics are designed for general text and may not be appropriate or meaningful for data-to-text corpora. No validation that these metrics correlate with generation difficulty or micro-planning complexity.
evidence: Section 4.2 uses CTTR, LS, and TTR without justifying their appropriateness for data-to-text evaluation
LS defined as proportion of lemmas not in 2000 most frequent words from BNC; may reflect rare entity names rather than linguistic sophistication
No correlation analysis between metrics and generation difficulty or seq2seq performance
No comparison with alternative complexity metrics (e.g., syntactic complexity, semantic complexity, input entropy)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate metric appropriateness by correlating CTTR, LS, TTR with seq2seq perplexity or BLEU scores. Analyze LS distribution by word class to separate entity names from linguistic sophistication. Consider alternative metrics (e.g., syntactic complexity, semantic complexity, input entropy).

concerns.title: Statistical significance not reported for key comparisons
concerns.description: The paper reports point estimates for dataset properties and text metrics but does not provide statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or effect sizes. Differences in text length (18.2 vs 16.8 tokens) and complexity metrics are modest and may not be statistically significant.
evidence: Table 4 reports DBPNLG 18.2 tokens/text vs RNNLG 16.8 (≈8% difference) without significance test
Table 4 reports DBPNLG 1.47 sentences/text vs RNNLG 1.23 (≈20% difference) without significance test
CTTR and LS differences are small (0.0649 vs 0.0589, 0.1847 vs 0.1523) without confidence intervals
No discussion of effect sizes or practical significance
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests for text length and complexity metrics. Report p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d). Discuss practical significance of differences.

concerns.title: Generalizability claims not empirically supported
concerns.description: The paper claims the framework is applicable to other RDF KBs (MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData) but provides no empirical evidence. Framework tested on only 6 DBpedia categories; applicability to other KBs is theoretical.
evidence: Section 3 states framework is 'generic' but tests only on DBpedia
Section 5 mentions 14 additional categories collected but not yet processed
No pilot study or feasibility analysis for other RDF KBs
No discussion of how framework handles KBs with different schema complexity, property types, or entity distributions
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct pilot study on at least one other RDF KB (e.g., MusicBrainz or FOAF). Apply framework to 1–2 categories and report results. Discuss challenges and adaptations needed. Provide evidence for generalizability claims.

concerns.title: Micro-planning support claimed but not directly evaluated
concerns.description: The paper claims DBPNLG supports learning of micro-planning subtasks (lexicalisation, aggregation, surface realisation, sentence segmentation, referring expression generation) but does not directly evaluate whether models trained on DBPNLG actually learn these subtasks. Support is inferred from dataset properties rather than task-specific evaluation.
evidence: Section 3 states: 'the resulting benchmark is appropriate for exercising the main subtasks of microplanning' but provides no direct evaluation
Example 1 illustrates how a single data-text pair involves multiple micro-planning subtasks, but this is anecdotal
Section 4.3 uses seq2seq model performance as proxy for complexity but does not evaluate whether models learn specific micro-planning subtasks
No error analysis or task-specific evaluation (e.g., lexicalisation accuracy, aggregation quality)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct task-specific evaluation of models trained on DBPNLG. Evaluate lexicalisation accuracy (e.g., correct property-to-word mappings), aggregation quality (e.g., use of coordination, ellipsis), surface realisation accuracy (e.g., syntactic correctness), sentence segmentation accuracy, and referring expression generation quality. Compare with models trained on RNNLG.

concerns.title: Balanced sampling may disadvantage RNNLG in fair comparison
concerns.description: The paper uses a balanced sample of 13K pairs for both datasets to ensure fair comparison, but this reduces RNNLG from its full size. RNNLG may benefit from larger training set, and the comparison may not reflect performance on original datasets at their natural scales.
evidence: Section 4.3 states: 'To allow for a fair comparison, we use a similar amount of data (13K data-text pairs) for both datasets'
RNNLG is 'bigger in size than DBPNLG' so balanced sample reduces RNNLG
No analysis of how performance scales with dataset size for each dataset
No comparison of performance on full RNNLG dataset
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report seq2seq performance on full RNNLG dataset (not just balanced sample). Analyze how performance scales with dataset size for both datasets. Discuss whether balanced sampling is appropriate or whether full-dataset comparison would be more informative.

concerns.title: Delexicalisation procedure may obscure dataset differences
concerns.description: The paper uses delexicalisation (replacing entities with generic terms) as preprocessing for seq2seq training, but this may remove important signals of complexity (e.g., rare entity names, long entity references). Exact token matching for delexicalisation may fail for paraphrased entities.
evidence: Section 4.3 describes two delexicalisation modes: full and name-only
Delexicalisation done via exact token match between entities and text
No analysis of delexicalisation success rate or failure cases
No discussion of how delexicalisation affects comparison between datasets
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report delexicalisation success rate for both datasets. Analyze failure cases (e.g., paraphrased entities, partial matches). Conduct seq2seq experiments without delexicalisation to assess impact. Discuss whether delexicalisation obscures or reveals dataset differences.

concerns.title: Crowdsourcing procedure may introduce bias toward certain aggregation patterns
concerns.description: The paper collects single-triple verbalisations first, then asks crowd to merge them into multi-triple texts. This procedure may bias toward certain aggregation patterns (e.g., simple concatenation, coordination) and may not reflect how humans naturally verbalise multi-triple inputs.
evidence: Section 3.3, Step 3 describes collecting single-triple verbalisations first, then merging them
Rationale: 'we diminish the risk of having misinterpretations of the original semantics of a data unit'
Contributors encouraged to 'change the order, and the wording of sentences' but starting from pre-written sentences may constrain possibilities
No comparison with direct multi-triple verbalisations
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct pilot study comparing texts produced by merging single-triple verbalisations vs. direct multi-triple verbalisations. Analyze aggregation patterns in both conditions. Assess whether merging procedure introduces bias.

concerns.title: Limited category coverage may not be representative
concerns.description: The paper tests framework on only 6 DBpedia categories (Astronaut, Building, Monument, University, Sports team, Written work). These categories may not be representative of DBpedia diversity in terms of property distributions, entity densities, or linguistic patterns.
evidence: Section 3.2 states: 'We applied this content selection procedure to the DBPedia categories Astronaut (A), Building (B), Monument (M), University (U), Sports team (S) and Written work (W)'
Section 5 mentions '14 further categories collected but not yet processed'
No analysis of category diversity or representativeness
No discussion of how results might differ for other categories
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze diversity of DBpedia categories in terms of property distributions, entity densities, and linguistic patterns. Assess whether 6 categories are representative. Process additional categories and report results to validate generalizability.

concerns.title: Attribute count comparison assumes semantic equivalence
concerns.description: The paper compares attribute counts (172 vs 108) but assumes direct semantic equivalence between RNNLG dialog-act attributes and DBpedia RDF properties. These may not be comparable; RNNLG attributes may be more abstract or domain-specific.
evidence: Section 4.1 states: 'The attributes in (Wen et al., 2016)'s dataset can be viewed as binary relations between the object talked about (a restaurant, a laptop, a TV or a hotel) and a value. Similarly, in DBPNLG, DBpedia RDF properties relate a subject entity to an object'
No analysis of semantic overlap or differences between attribute types
Example 3 shows different lexicalisations for attributes but does not validate comparability
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze semantic overlap between RNNLG attributes and DBpedia properties. Map attributes to properties where possible. Discuss non-comparable attributes. Provide adjusted comparison accounting for semantic differences.

comparable_works.relevance: Direct comparison baseline; crowdsourced data-to-text corpus using enumeration-based content selection
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar: both crowdsourced, both data-to-text, both for NLG. Different: RNNLG uses enumeration of dialog acts; DBPNLG uses ILP-based selection from RDF. RNNLG is larger (531K tokens) but less diverse.
comparable_works.source_trace: Wen et al. (2016) cited throughout; Section 2, Section 4

comparable_works.citation_label: Perez-Beltrachini et al. (2016) content selection procedure
comparable_works.relevance: Methodological foundation; ILP-based content selection from RDF graphs using bigram coherence models
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar: same ILP formulation and bigram models. Different: Perez-Beltrachini et al. focus on content selection; this paper combines with crowdsourcing for corpus creation.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 3.2 cites Perez-Beltrachini et al. (2016) as foundation for content selection procedure

comparable_works.relevance: Related work on crowdsourced data-to-text corpus creation with automatic quality control
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar: crowdsourcing for data-to-text, quality control measures. Different: Novikova and Rieser focus on impact of input representation (text vs pictures); this paper focuses on content selection and linguistic diversity.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2 cites Novikova and Rieser (2016) as example of crowdsourced benchmark

comparable_works.relevance: Expert-annotated NLG benchmark; alternative approach to corpus creation
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Different: AMR uses expert annotation of complex linguistic structures; DBPNLG uses crowdsourcing from automatically-selected data. AMR supports surface realisation; DBPNLG supports micro-planning.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2 discusses AMR as example of expert-annotated benchmark

comparable_works.citation_label: Belz et al. (2011) SR'11 Surface Realisation task
comparable_works.relevance: Expert-annotated NLG benchmark derived from dependency parse trees
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Different: SR'11 uses parse trees as input; DBPNLG uses RDF triples. SR'11 focuses on surface realisation; DBPNLG supports micro-planning.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2 discusses SR'11 as example of expert-annotated benchmark

comparable_works.citation_label: Chen and Mooney (2008) sports domain corpus
comparable_works.relevance: Domain-specific data-to-text corpus; example of limited-scope NLG benchmark
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Different: domain-specific (sports) vs. wide-coverage (DBpedia). Chen and Mooney focus on single domain; DBPNLG supports multiple categories.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2 cites Chen and Mooney (2008) as example of domain-specific corpus

comparable_works.citation_label: Vinyals et al. (2015) seq2seq with attention
comparable_works.relevance: Neural baseline model for evaluating dataset complexity
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Used as evaluation tool; not a comparable corpus. Seq2seq is standard architecture for data-to-text generation.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 4.3 uses Vinyals et al. (2015) seq2seq model for performance comparison

uncertainty_flags: Generalizability of framework: tested on only 6 DBpedia categories; applicability to other RDF KBs is theoretical, not empirically demonstrated
Coherence validation: bigram probability used as proxy for coherence; no direct human evaluation of selected units' coherence or relevance
Crowdsourcing quality: inter-annotator agreement not reported; 8.7% loss rate suggests remaining errors; quality may vary across categories

Causal claims about complexity: lower seq2seq performance attributed to dataset complexity, but alternative explanations (model architecture, hyperparameters, vocabulary mismatch, delexicalisation artifacts) not ruled out
Metric appropriateness: CTTR, LS, TTR designed for general text; validity for data-to-text corpora not established; no correlation with generation difficulty demonstrated
Micro-planning support: claimed but not directly evaluated; no task-specific evaluation of lexicalisation, aggregation, surface realisation, sentence segmentation, referring expression generation
Statistical significance: text length and complexity differences are modest; no significance tests reported; confidence intervals missing
Balanced sampling: comparison uses 13K pairs for both datasets; RNNLG reduced from full size, potentially disadvantaging it if it benefits from scale
Error analysis: no detailed analysis of seq2seq errors; unclear whether lower performance reflects genuine complexity or dataset-specific phenomena
Delexicalisation effects: exact token matching may fail for paraphrased entities; impact on comparison unclear
Attribute comparability: assumes direct semantic equivalence between RNNLG dialog-act attributes and DBpedia RDF properties; not validated
Category representativeness: 6 categories may not be representative of DBpedia diversity; 14 additional categories collected but not yet processed
ILP reproducibility: incomplete specification of ILP formulation, solver parameters, and convergence criteria limits reproducibility
Crowdsourcing bias: merging single-triple verbalisations may bias toward certain aggregation patterns; no comparison with direct multi-triple verbalisations
alternative_interpretations: Lower seq2seq performance on DBPNLG may reflect model-dataset mismatch rather than inherent complexity. Seq2seq models may be poorly suited for both datasets; alternative architectures (e.g., structured models, hierarchical models) might show different performance patterns.

Higher CTTR and LS in DBPNLG may reflect rare entity names (proper nouns) rather than linguistic sophistication. Breakdown by word class could reveal that most high-LS words are named entities, not sophisticated vocabulary.
Diversity in input shapes and attributes may not translate to learning difficulty. Models may learn to ignore rare shapes or attributes; diversity does not necessarily improve generalization.

Bigram coherence models may capture statistical patterns that do not correspond to semantic coherence. ILP-selected units may be statistically coherent but pragmatically irrelevant or semantically incoherent.

Crowdsourcing procedure (merging single-triple verbalisations) may produce unnatural aggregation patterns. Texts may be less natural than direct multi-triple verbalisations, biasing toward certain syntactic constructs.
Attribute count comparison may be misleading. RNNLG attributes may be more abstract or domain-specific; direct count comparison may not reflect semantic diversity.
8.7% corpus loss during verification may introduce bias. Rejected pairs may have systematic properties (e.g., longer texts, rare attributes) that affect representativeness of final dataset.
Generalizability claims may be overstated. Framework may be specific to DBpedia's schema and entity distributions; applicability to other RDF KBs may require significant adaptations.
transparency_notes: Paper acknowledges that only 6 out of 14 collected categories have been processed, indicating preliminary nature of evaluation.
Paper acknowledges that seq2seq models may not be optimal for complex texts, suggesting need for alternative architectures.
Paper commits to releasing DBPNLG as part of shared task, supporting reproducibility and community evaluation.
Paper does not report inter-annotator agreement metrics, limiting assessment of crowdsourcing quality.
Paper does not provide complete ILP specification, limiting reproducibility of content selection procedure.
Paper does not conduct error analysis of seq2seq outputs, limiting understanding of performance differences.
Paper does not validate appropriateness of complexity metrics (CTTR, LS) for data-to-text corpora.
Paper does not report statistical significance tests or confidence intervals for key comparisons.
Paper does not directly evaluate micro-planning support; claims are inferred from dataset properties.
Paper does not provide pilot study or feasibility analysis for applicability to other RDF KBs.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The combination of ILP-based content selection with crowdsourcing for corpus generation is novel and represents a meaningful methodological contribution. However, novelty does not guarantee validity. The paper's claims about dataset suitability for micro-planning and applicability to other RDF KBs are not adequately supported by evidence. Methodological flaws (missing IAA metrics, incomplete ILP specification, unvalidated assumptions) undermine confidence in the contribution, independent of its novelty.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If inter-annotator agreement metrics were reported and showed high agreement (kappa > 0.7), confidence in crowdsourcing quality would increase.
If direct human evaluation of coherence and relevance for ILP-selected units showed high scores, the bigram coherence assumption would be validated.
If task-specific evaluation demonstrated that models trained on DBPNLG learn micro-planning subtasks better than models trained on RNNLG, the micro-planning support claim would be supported.
If pilot study on another RDF KB (e.g., MusicBrainz) showed successful application of framework, generalizability claims would be validated.
If error analysis of seq2seq outputs showed that errors reflect complexity (e.g., rare structures, complex aggregation) rather than other factors, the complexity claim would be strengthened.
If statistical significance tests showed that text length and complexity differences are meaningful (p < 0.05, large effect sizes), the complexity comparison would be more convincing.
If alternative model architectures (e.g., structured models) showed similar performance patterns, the seq2seq results would be more robust.
If ablation study compared S-Model, C-Model, and M-Model, the contribution of each bigram model to diversity and coherence would be clarified.

novelty_lenses.lens: Incremental innovation in corpus generation methodology
novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper combines existing techniques (ILP-based content selection from Perez-Beltrachini et al. 2016, crowdsourcing from Wen et al. 2016) in a new way. The combination is creative and addresses real limitations of existing approaches, but individual components are not novel. The contribution is primarily in the integration and application to corpus generation.
evidence: ILP-based content selection is from Perez-Beltrachini et al. (2016)
Crowdsourcing approach is similar to Wen et al. (2016) but with different content selection
Combination of ILP and crowdsourcing for corpus generation is novel
Application to DBpedia and RDF KBs is new
uncertainty_flags: Novelty of combination is somewhat limited; both components are established techniques
Contribution is primarily methodological (corpus generation) rather than algorithmic or theoretical
Applicability to other RDF KBs is claimed but not demonstrated

novelty_lenses.rationale: The DBPNLG dataset is a new resource that addresses a gap in NLG benchmarks. While data-to-text corpora exist (RNNLG, domain-specific corpora), DBPNLG is novel in combining RDF data from a large KB (DBpedia) with crowdsourced text. The dataset is designed to support micro-planning and wide-coverage generation, which is a new focus.
evidence: DBPNLG is a new dataset combining DBpedia RDF data with crowdsourced text
Dataset is designed to support micro-planning and wide-coverage generation
Dataset exhibits greater linguistic diversity than existing benchmarks (RNNLG)
Dataset will be released as part of shared task, enabling community evaluation
uncertainty_flags: Dataset is relatively small (290K tokens) compared to RNNLG (531K tokens)
Only 6 DBpedia categories processed; full dataset not yet available
Novelty of dataset depends on whether linguistic diversity translates to practical utility for NLG

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper provides a comprehensive comparative analysis of DBPNLG and RNNLG across multiple dimensions. This analysis is thorough and informative, but the findings are somewhat expected: smaller, more diverse datasets are harder to learn from. The empirical contribution is primarily in quantifying and documenting these differences.
evidence: Comprehensive comparison across 5 dataset properties and 6 text properties
Seq2seq performance comparison on both datasets
Multiple metrics and examples illustrating differences
Analysis is systematic and well-organized
uncertainty_flags: Findings are somewhat expected; lower performance on more diverse dataset is not surprising
Empirical contribution is primarily in quantification rather than new insights
Causal claims about complexity are not adequately supported

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper does not introduce new theoretical concepts or frameworks. The connection between input structure (depth, shape, attributes) and syntactic complexity is intuitive and well-known in NLG. The paper applies existing concepts to a new dataset but does not advance theoretical understanding.
evidence: Figure 1 illustrates intuitive connection between input structure and syntax (path vs. branching)
Examples 3 and 4 show how attributes induce different syntactic realisations (well-known in NLG)
No new theoretical frameworks or concepts introduced
Paper is primarily empirical and methodological
uncertainty_flags: Lack of theoretical novelty is not necessarily a weakness for a resource paper
Empirical validation of intuitive concepts can be valuable

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper makes a solid methodological contribution (combining ILP and crowdsourcing for corpus generation) and provides a useful resource (DBPNLG dataset). However, several methodological concerns limit confidence: (1) unvalidated assumptions (bigram probability = coherence, crowdsourcing quality), (2) incomplete technical specifications (ILP formulation), (3) indirect validation of key claims (micro-planning support, complexity), (4) limited generalizability evidence (6 categories only), (5) missing statistical rigor (no significance tests, IAA metrics). The paper is above the threshold for acceptance as a resource paper with methodological contribution, but the methodological flaws and limited evidence for key claims prevent higher confidence. The contribution is meaningful but not exceptional; the execution is competent but has notable gaps.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper presents a semi-automatic framework for creating data-to-text corpora from RDF knowledge bases (specifically DBpedia) to support training of wide-coverage NLG micro-planners. The contribution is incremental but meaningful: it refines and extends the crowdsourcing-based corpus creation paradigm established by Wen et al. (2016) by introducing (1) ILP-based content selection over RDF category graphs to produce more diverse input shapes and patterns, and (2) a four-step crowdsourcing procedure that combines single-triple verbalisations with multi-triple merging. The paper's core novelty lies not in inventing new techniques (ILP for content selection and crowdsourcing are established methods) but in their combination and application to RDF data, and in the empirical demonstration that smaller, more diverse datasets can be more challenging for seq2seq models than larger, repetitive ones. The work occupies a clear position within the data-to-text NLG literature: it addresses acknowledged limitations of Wen et al. (2016) (artificial data, shallow input trees, limited linguistic diversity) through targeted methodological refinements. However, the innovation is primarily architectural and empirical rather than conceptual. The paper makes a solid incremental advance by showing that diversity metrics and input shape variation matter for NLG learning, but this insight emerges from careful engineering of existing methods rather than from fundamentally new ideas.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: Existing crowdsourced NLG benchmarks (Wen et al. 2016) use artificial data from hand-written ontologies, limiting applicability to KB verbalisers.
Premise 2: Wen et al. (2016) inputs are shallow trees (depth 1), which restrict syntactic diversity and do not exercise complex micro-planning operations.
Premise 3: Content selection via enumeration of dialog acts produces repetitive datasets (high input/pattern ratio), which may induce overfitting and limit generalization.
Conclusion 1: A framework combining RDF-based content selection (ILP over category graphs) and crowdsourcing can address these limitations.
Premise 4: ILP-based selection using bigram coherence models can produce varied, relevant data units from real KB data.
Premise 5: Crowdsourcing with majority-vote validation ensures semantic adequacy and grammaticality.

Conclusion 2: The resulting DBPNLG dataset exhibits greater linguistic and semantic diversity than RNNLG across multiple dimensions (attributes, input patterns, input shapes, tree depth, text length, lexical diversity).
Premise 6: Lower seq2seq performance on DBPNLG (higher perplexity, lower BLEU) indicates greater learning difficulty.
Conclusion 3: DBPNLG is more challenging and suitable for training wide-coverage micro-planners despite being smaller than RNNLG.
Implicit Premise 7: Smaller, more diverse datasets are preferable to larger, repetitive ones for learning generalizable NLG systems.
Implicit Conclusion 4: The framework is generalizable to other RDF knowledge bases (MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData).

identified_claims.claim_label: Semi-automatic framework creates suitable corpora
identified_claims.claim_text: A semi-automatic framework combining content selection (via ILP over DBpedia category graphs) and crowdsourcing can create data-to-text corpora suitable for training KB verbalisers and micro-planners.
evidence: Section 3 introduces the framework combining ILP-based content selection and crowdsourcing
Section 3.2 describes ILP formulation for selecting subtrees with maximal bigram probability
Section 3.3 details four-step crowdsourcing procedure (property clarification, single-triple verbalisations, multi-triple merging, quality verification)
Example 1 demonstrates a data/text pair created by the method
uncertainty_flags: Framework tested on only 6 DBpedia categories; generalizability to other RDF KBs claimed but not empirically demonstrated
Crowdsourcing quality control relies on manual post-hoc checks; no inter-annotator agreement metrics reported
8.7% corpus loss during verification step; impact on final dataset representativeness not discussed
No direct evaluation of whether corpus actually supports training of micro-planners; suitability inferred from dataset properties rather than task-specific evaluation

identified_claims.claim_label: DBPNLG exhibits greater linguistic diversity than RNNLG
identified_claims.claim_text: The resulting DBPNLG dataset, though smaller than Wen et al. (2016)'s RNNLG dataset, exhibits significantly greater linguistic and semantic diversity across multiple dimensions: more attributes (172 vs 108), more input patterns (58 distinct shapes vs 6), lower input-pattern repetition ratio (2.40 vs 10.31), and deeper input trees (depth up to 5 vs depth 1).
evidence: Table 3 reports: DBPNLG 172 attributes vs RNNLG 108; DBPNLG 58 input shapes vs RNNLG 6
Table 3 reports: DBPNLG input/pattern ratio 2.40 vs RNNLG 10.31
Section 4.1 states RNNLG inputs are trees of depth 1; DBPNLG inputs have depth up to 5 with 49.6% of inputs having depth > 1
Examples 3 and 4 illustrate how different attributes induce different syntactic realisations
uncertainty_flags: Attribute count comparison assumes direct equivalence between RNNLG dialog-act attributes and DBpedia RDF properties; semantic comparability not established
Input shape diversity measured by count of distinct shapes; no analysis of whether all 58 shapes are linguistically meaningful or some are rare artifacts
Claim that deeper trees 'favour' certain syntactic constructs (Section 3, Figure 1) is intuitive but not empirically validated on the actual datasets
Statistical significance of differences not reported; modest differences in some metrics (e.g., text length 18.2 vs 16.8 tokens)

identified_claims.claim_label: DBPNLG texts are more complex and linguistically sophisticated
identified_claims.claim_text: DBPNLG texts are more complex and linguistically sophisticated: longer (more tokens and sentences per text), higher lexical diversity (CTTR), higher lexical sophistication (LS), and larger vocabulary relative to corpus size.
evidence: Table 4 reports: DBPNLG 18.2 tokens/text vs RNNLG 16.8; DBPNLG 1.47 sentences/text vs RNNLG 1.23
Table 4 reports: DBPNLG CTTR 0.0649 vs RNNLG 0.0589; DBPNLG LS 0.1847 vs RNNLG 0.1523
Table 4 reports: DBPNLG 2992 types / 290479 tokens vs RNNLG 3524 types / 531871 tokens (proportionally higher vocabulary in DBPNLG)
Examples 5 and 6 illustrate text length and complexity differences
uncertainty_flags: Text length differences are modest (18.2 vs 16.8 tokens, 1.47 vs 1.23 sentences); statistical significance not reported
CTTR and LS are computed using external tool (Lu 2012); no validation that these metrics are appropriate for data-to-text corpora or correlate with generation difficulty
Vocabulary comparison conflates absolute size (RNNLG has more types) with relative size (DBPNLG has higher type/token ratio); interpretation depends on learning objective
Higher LS in DBPNLG may reflect rare entity names (proper nouns) rather than linguistic sophistication; no analysis of LS composition

identified_claims.claim_label: Increased complexity validated by lower seq2seq performance
identified_claims.claim_text: The increased complexity of DBPNLG is empirically validated by lower sequence-to-sequence model performance (higher perplexity and lower BLEU), indicating a more challenging learning task that better exercises micro-planning subtasks (lexicalisation, aggregation, surface realisation, sentence segmentation, referring expression generation).
evidence: Table 5 reports: DBPNLG perplexity 8.47 (full delexicalisation) vs RNNLG 6.89; DBPNLG 7.21 (name-only) vs RNNLG 5.89
Table 5 reports: DBPNLG BLEU 0.3891 vs RNNLG 0.4582 (full delexicalisation); DBPNLG 0.4156 vs RNNLG 0.5123 (name-only)
Section 4.3 uses Vinyals et al. (2015) seq2seq model with attention; balanced sample of 13K pairs used for fair comparison
Section 5 concludes that DBPNLG is 'more challenging for such models'
uncertainty_flags: Causal claim (complexity → lower performance) assumes lower performance is solely due to dataset properties, not model architecture or hyperparameter choices
Balanced sample of 13K pairs reduces RNNLG from its full size; comparison is not on original datasets at their natural scales; RNNLG may benefit from scale
Perplexity and BLEU are indirect proxies for 'exercising micro-planning subtasks'; no direct evaluation of whether models actually learn lexicalisation, aggregation, etc.
No error analysis provided; unclear whether lower performance reflects genuine complexity or dataset-specific phenomena (e.g., rare vocabulary, unusual structures, delexicalisation mismatches)
Seq2seq may not be optimal for either dataset; no comparison with other architectures or task-specific models

identified_claims.claim_label: RDF-based content selection produces varied and coherent data units
identified_claims.claim_text: RDF-based content selection using bigram coherence models (sibling, chain, and mixed) produces more varied and coherent data units than enumeration of dialog acts and attribute combinations.
evidence: Section 3.2 describes three bigram models (S-Model for siblings, C-Model for chains, M-Model for mixed) learned from category graphs
Section 3.2 formulates content selection as ILP to select subtrees with maximal bigram probability
Table 1 shows results across 6 categories and 3 bigram models with varying triple counts (1–7)
Section 3 contrasts this with Wen et al. (2016)'s enumeration approach
uncertainty_flags: No direct comparison of coherence between ILP-selected units and enumerated units; 'coherence' is assumed to follow from bigram probability but not validated
Bigram models trained on category graphs; unclear how well these capture coherence for out-of-category entities or cross-category relations
Table 1 reports counts of inputs and patterns but does not evaluate coherence, relevance, or semantic adequacy of selected units
ILP formulation details (objective function, constraints, solver parameters) not fully specified; reproducibility unclear
No ablation study comparing ILP-based selection with simpler alternatives

identified_claims.claim_label: Framework applicable to other RDF knowledge bases
identified_claims.claim_text: The framework can be used to create a data-to-text corpus from any knowledge base where entities are categorised and there is a large number of entities belonging to the same category, and could be applied to e.g., MusicBrainz, FOAF or LinkedGeoData.
evidence: Section 3 states: 'it can be used to create a data-to-text corpus from any knowledge base where entities are categorised and there is a large number of entities belonging to the same category'
Section 5 mentions 'many large scale datasets are encoded in the RDF language (e.g., MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData)'
Section 3 notes the framework is 'generic' and applicable beyond DBpedia
uncertainty_flags: Generalizability claim is theoretical; framework tested only on DBpedia with 6 categories
Applicability to other RDF KBs depends on availability of category hierarchies and sufficient entity density; not all RDF KBs have these properties
Crowdsourcing procedure includes manual property clarification step (Section 3.3); effort required for other KBs not estimated
No evidence that bigram coherence models trained on one KB transfer to another
Framework assumes English; applicability to multilingual KBs (e.g., multilingual DBpedia) not discussed

strengths.title: Clear problem motivation and positioning within NLG literature
strengths.description: The paper clearly articulates limitations of existing crowdsourced benchmarks (Wen et al. 2016) and positions the contribution as addressing specific gaps: artificial data, shallow input trees, limited linguistic diversity. This positioning is well-grounded in the data-to-text NLG literature and makes the incremental nature of the contribution transparent.
evidence: Section 2 provides comprehensive review of three types of NLG benchmarks (domain-specific, expert-annotated, crowdsourced)
Section 3 explicitly identifies shortcomings of Wen et al. (2016) and proposes targeted solutions
Introduction clearly states focus on wide-coverage micro-planners and specific NLG subtasks

strengths.title: Comprehensive empirical comparison across multiple linguistic dimensions
strengths.description: The paper provides a thorough comparative analysis of DBPNLG vs. RNNLG across diverse metrics: attributes, input patterns, input shapes, tree depth, text length, lexical diversity (CTTR), lexical sophistication (LS), and neural model performance. This multi-dimensional evaluation strengthens the empirical foundation for claims about dataset diversity.
evidence: Table 3 reports 7 distinct data-related metrics with clear numerical comparisons
Table 4 reports 6 text-related metrics with detailed statistics
Table 5 provides neural model performance across two delexicalisation modes
Examples 3-6 illustrate linguistic phenomena with concrete data-text pairs

strengths.title: Methodologically sound crowdsourcing procedure with quality control
strengths.description: The four-step crowdsourcing procedure (property clarification, single-triple verbalisations, multi-triple merging, quality verification) is well-designed to minimize semantic misalignment between data and text. The use of majority-vote validation and manual post-hoc checks demonstrates attention to data quality.
evidence: Section 3.3 details four-step procedure with clear rationale for each step
Automatic validators (12 custom javascript checks) prevent spamming and enforce quality standards
Manual checks eliminate mismatched pairs; 8.7% corpus loss indicates non-trivial quality filtering
Merging single-triple verbalisations reduces risk of semantic misinterpretation

strengths.title: Practical applicability to real knowledge bases
strengths.description: Unlike Wen et al. (2016) which uses artificial hand-written ontologies, the framework operates on real RDF data from DBpedia. This enables training of KB verbalisers, which is a genuine practical need as institutions increasingly publish data in RDF format.
evidence: Framework uses real DBpedia data with 6.2M entities, 739 classes, 1,099 properties
Section 5 notes that 'official institutions increasingly publish their data in this format'
Example 1 demonstrates realistic data-text pair from DBpedia
Framework explicitly designed for KB verbalisers, addressing a gap in existing benchmarks

strengths.title: Well-motivated use of ILP for content selection
strengths.description: The application of ILP to select subtrees with maximal bigram probability is well-motivated by the goal of producing varied, coherent data units. The use of three bigram models (sibling, chain, mixed) captures different types of coherence and is theoretically grounded.
evidence: Section 3.2 provides clear intuition for three bigram models: 'topic-based coherence for the S-Model and discourse-based coherence for the C-Model'
ILP formulation allows flexible control over data unit size (1-7 triples) and model selection
Figure 1 illustrates how input shape (path vs. branching) correlates with syntactic structure, motivating the need for diverse input shapes
Table 1 shows results across multiple categories and models, demonstrating systematic application

strengths.title: Transparent reporting of dataset statistics and corpus loss
strengths.description: The paper transparently reports dataset statistics (Table 1, Table 3, Table 4) and acknowledges corpus loss (8.7% during verification). This transparency enables readers to assess data quality and make informed judgments about dataset suitability.
evidence: Table 1 reports inputs, patterns, properties, entities for each category and bigram model
Table 3 provides detailed comparison of DBPNLG and RNNLG across multiple dimensions
Section 3.3 explicitly states '8.7% corpus loss was of 8.7%' after verification
Examples 1-6 provide concrete data-text pairs for inspection

strengths.title: Addresses genuine limitation of existing benchmarks regarding input shape diversity
strengths.description: The observation that RNNLG inputs are shallow trees (depth 1) while DBPNLG inputs have depth up to 5 is a genuine and important distinction. Deeper trees do enable more diverse syntactic constructions (object relative clauses, passive participials) as illustrated in Figure 1, addressing a real gap in existing benchmarks.
evidence: Figure 1 clearly illustrates how path vs. branching structures favour different syntactic constructs
Section 4.1 reports RNNLG has only 6 distinct shapes (all depth 1) vs. DBPNLG 58 shapes (49.6% depth > 1)
Examples 4a and 4b show how different attribute sets induce different syntactic realisations
This distinction is theoretically motivated and empirically demonstrated

concerns.title: Lack of inter-annotator agreement metrics for crowdsourcing quality
concerns.description: The paper reports crowdsourcing procedures and an 8.7% corpus loss rate but does not provide inter-annotator agreement (IAA) metrics (e.g., Cohen's kappa, Fleiss' kappa) for the majority-vote validation step. This omission makes it difficult to assess the reliability of crowdsourced annotations and compare quality with other crowdsourced datasets.
evidence: Section 3.3 describes majority-vote validation but does not report IAA metrics
No comparison of crowdsourcing quality with Wen et al. (2016) or other benchmarks
8.7% corpus loss is reported but not contextualized (is this high or low?)
No analysis of which types of pairs were rejected or why
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report inter-annotator agreement metrics (Cohen's kappa or Fleiss' kappa) for the majority-vote validation step. Provide breakdown of corpus loss by category and reason (fluency, semantic adequacy, grammaticality). Compare IAA with Wen et al. (2016) if possible.

concerns.title: Statistical significance of reported differences not established
concerns.description: The paper reports numerical differences between DBPNLG and RNNLG (e.g., 18.2 vs. 16.8 tokens/text, 1.47 vs. 1.23 sentences/text) but does not provide statistical significance tests (t-tests, chi-square tests, etc.). Some differences are modest and may not be statistically significant, particularly for text length metrics.
evidence: Table 4 reports text length differences without significance tests
Differences in tokens/text (18.2 vs. 16.8) and sentences/text (1.47 vs. 1.23) are modest
No confidence intervals or p-values reported for any metrics
Section 4.2 uses language like 'DBPNLG's texts are longer' without quantifying uncertainty
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct statistical significance tests (t-tests for continuous metrics, chi-square for categorical) and report p-values and confidence intervals. Clarify which differences are statistically significant and which are merely numerically larger.

concerns.title: Appropriateness of CTTR and LS metrics for data-to-text evaluation not validated
concerns.description: The paper uses CTTR (corrected type-token ratio) and LS (lexical sophistication) as measures of linguistic diversity and sophistication. These metrics are designed for general text and their appropriateness for data-to-text corpora is not established. No validation that these metrics correlate with generation difficulty or are meaningful for NLG tasks.
evidence: Section 4.2 uses CTTR and LS without justifying their appropriateness for data-to-text corpora
LS defined as proportion of lemmas not in 2000 most frequent BNC words; may conflate rare entities with linguistic sophistication
No correlation analysis between LS/CTTR and seq2seq performance or generation difficulty
Metrics borrowed from general text analysis (Lu 2012) without adaptation for NLG
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate that CTTR and LS correlate with generation difficulty (e.g., seq2seq perplexity). Alternatively, propose NLG-specific diversity metrics. Analyze composition of LS to distinguish rare entities from genuinely sophisticated language.

concerns.title: Balanced sampling may disadvantage RNNLG in neural model comparison
concerns.description: The neural model comparison uses a balanced sample of 13K pairs for both datasets. Since RNNLG is larger (531K tokens vs. 290K), reducing it to 13K pairs may disadvantage RNNLG if it benefits from scale. The comparison is not on the original datasets at their natural scales, which may bias results.
evidence: Section 4.3 states: 'To allow for a fair comparison, we use a similar amount of data (13K data-text pairs) for both datasets'
RNNLG is 'bigger in size than DBPNLG', so balanced sampling reduces RNNLG significantly
No analysis of how performance scales with dataset size for each dataset
Comparison is not on original datasets; unclear if 13K is fair for both
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report neural model performance on both original dataset sizes and on balanced samples. Provide learning curves showing how performance scales with dataset size for each dataset. Discuss whether balanced sampling is appropriate or whether comparison should account for dataset size differences.

concerns.title: No error analysis of seq2seq model performance differences
concerns.description: The paper reports lower seq2seq performance on DBPNLG (higher perplexity, lower BLEU) but provides no error analysis. It is unclear whether lower performance reflects genuine dataset complexity or dataset-specific phenomena (e.g., rare vocabulary, unusual structures, delexicalisation mismatches, out-of-vocabulary words).
evidence: Section 4.3 reports perplexity and BLEU but does not analyze errors
No breakdown of errors by type (vocabulary, structure, alignment, etc.)
No analysis of which inputs or texts are harder for the model
Claim that DBPNLG 'exercises micro-planning subtasks' is not directly validated
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide error analysis of seq2seq predictions on both datasets. Categorize errors (e.g., OOV words, missing aggregation, incorrect lexicalisation). Analyze which dataset properties correlate with error rates. Consider task-specific evaluation of micro-planning subtasks (lexicalisation, aggregation, etc.).

concerns.title: Causal claim about complexity not adequately supported
concerns.description: The paper claims that lower seq2seq performance on DBPNLG indicates that DBPNLG is 'more challenging' and 'more complex'. However, this causal claim assumes that lower performance is solely due to dataset properties, not model architecture, hyperparameter choices, or other factors. Alternative explanations are not ruled out.
evidence: Section 4.3 uses same seq2seq model for both datasets; hyperparameters not tuned per dataset
Section 5 concludes: 'data-to-text corpora built by our framework are challenging for such models'
No comparison with other model architectures (e.g., structured models, hierarchical models)
No analysis of whether seq2seq is optimal for either dataset
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Acknowledge that lower seq2seq performance may reflect model-dataset mismatch rather than inherent dataset complexity. Compare with other model architectures. Discuss whether seq2seq is appropriate for evaluating dataset complexity. Consider task-specific metrics (e.g., lexicalisation accuracy, aggregation success) as more direct measures of complexity.

concerns.title: Generalizability of framework tested on only 6 DBpedia categories
concerns.description: The framework is claimed to be 'generic' and applicable to any RDF knowledge base with categorised entities. However, it is tested on only 6 DBpedia categories (Astronaut, Building, Monument, University, Sports team, Written work). The paper mentions 14 additional categories collected but not yet processed, suggesting the evaluation is preliminary.
evidence: Section 3.2 states: 'We applied this content selection procedure to the DBPedia categories Astronaut (A), Building (B), Monument (M), University (U), Sports team (S) and Written work (W)'
Section 5 notes: 'we have collected content for 14 further categories using the content selection procedure'
No analysis of whether 6 categories are representative of DBpedia diversity
Generalizability to other RDF KBs (MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData) is theoretical, not empirical
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Expand evaluation to include the 14 additional categories mentioned. Analyze whether results generalize across categories or if category-specific properties affect dataset diversity. Provide evidence of applicability to at least one other RDF knowledge base (e.g., MusicBrainz) to support generalizability claims.

concerns.title: Bigram coherence assumption not empirically validated
concerns.description: The paper assumes that bigram probability over RDF properties is a valid proxy for coherence and relevance of selected data units. However, this assumption is not empirically validated. No direct evaluation of whether ILP-selected units are actually more coherent or relevant than enumerated units.
evidence: Section 3.2 describes bigram models but does not validate that bigram probability correlates with coherence
Table 1 reports counts of inputs and patterns but not coherence or relevance metrics
No comparison of coherence between ILP-selected and enumerated units
Intuition provided ('topic-based coherence', 'discourse-based coherence') is not quantified
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct human evaluation of coherence and relevance for ILP-selected vs. enumerated data units. Measure inter-annotator agreement on coherence judgments. Correlate bigram probability with human coherence ratings to validate the assumption.

concerns.title: Attribute equivalence between DBPNLG and RNNLG not established
concerns.description: The paper compares attribute counts (172 vs. 108) but does not establish semantic equivalence between RNNLG dialog-act attributes and DBpedia RDF properties. These may represent fundamentally different types of information, making direct comparison problematic.
evidence: Section 4.1 refers to both as 'attributes' but notes they are 'binary relations' in different contexts
RNNLG attributes are dialog acts (e.g., 'request', 'inform') and attribute-value pairs
DBPNLG attributes are RDF properties (e.g., 'birthDate', 'occupation')
No analysis of semantic overlap or comparability
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the semantic relationship between RNNLG dialog-act attributes and DBPNLG RDF properties. Provide examples of equivalent attributes if they exist. Discuss whether attribute count is a meaningful comparison metric given the different nature of the two attribute types.

concerns.title: No direct evaluation of micro-planning support
concerns.description: The paper claims that DBPNLG 'better exercises micro-planning subtasks' (lexicalisation, aggregation, surface realisation, sentence segmentation, referring expression generation) but provides no direct evaluation. Support for this claim is indirect (dataset properties, seq2seq performance) rather than task-specific.
evidence: Section 3 lists micro-planning subtasks but does not evaluate whether DBPNLG supports learning them
Example 1 illustrates how generating (1b) from (1a) involves micro-planning, but this is anecdotal
Section 4.3 uses seq2seq perplexity and BLEU as indirect proxies for complexity
No task-specific evaluation (e.g., lexicalisation accuracy, aggregation success)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct task-specific evaluation of micro-planning subtasks. For example, evaluate whether models trained on DBPNLG can correctly lexicalise properties, aggregate information, and generate referring expressions. Compare performance on DBPNLG vs. RNNLG for each subtask.

concerns.title: Delexicalisation procedure may obscure dataset differences
concerns.description: The neural model comparison uses delexicalisation (replacing entities with generic terms). This preprocessing step may remove important signals of complexity (e.g., rare entity names, long entity references) and may not reflect real-world generation where entities are not delexicalised.
evidence: Section 4.3 describes two delexicalisation modes: full and name-only
Delexicalisation done via exact token match; may fail for paraphrased entities
Section 4.1 notes that 'at training time, different instantiations of the same input pattern reduce to identical input' after delexicalisation
No analysis of impact of delexicalisation on dataset differences
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report seq2seq performance without delexicalisation to assess impact. Analyze how delexicalisation affects dataset properties and model performance. Discuss whether delexicalisation is appropriate for evaluating dataset complexity.

concerns.title: Input shape diversity metric may include rare or uninformative patterns
concerns.description: The paper reports 58 distinct input shapes in DBPNLG vs. 6 in RNNLG as evidence of diversity. However, no analysis of whether all 58 shapes are linguistically meaningful or if some are rare artifacts that contribute little to linguistic diversity.
evidence: Section 4.1 reports 58 distinct shapes but does not analyze their distribution
No information on frequency of each shape (e.g., how many inputs have each shape)
No analysis of whether rare shapes are linguistically distinct or just noise
Figure 1 illustrates two shapes but does not show distribution across all 58
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide distribution of input shapes (frequency histogram). Analyze whether rare shapes contribute meaningfully to linguistic diversity or are artifacts. Consider reporting effective number of shapes (e.g., using entropy) rather than raw count.

concerns.title: Correlation between input shape and syntactic structure not empirically validated
concerns.description: The paper claims that input shape (tree depth and structure) correlates with syntactic complexity (Section 3, Figure 1). This claim is intuitive but not empirically validated on the actual datasets. No quantitative analysis of correlation between input shape and syntactic structure.
evidence: Figure 1 illustrates two shapes (path vs. branching) and their hypothesized syntactic effects
Section 3 states: 'there is a strong correlation between the shape of the input and the syntactic structure of the corresponding sentence'
Examples 4a and 4b show different attribute sets inducing different syntactic realisations
No quantitative correlation analysis (e.g., Pearson correlation, regression)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct quantitative analysis of correlation between input shape properties (depth, branching factor, etc.) and syntactic properties of generated text (sentence structure, clause types, etc.). Use linguistic parsing to extract syntactic features and correlate with input shape.

concerns.title: Crowdsourcing merging procedure may produce unnatural text
concerns.description: The crowdsourcing procedure (Section 3.3, Step 3) asks workers to merge pre-written single-triple verbalisations into multi-triple texts. This procedure may produce unnatural text with awkward transitions or redundancy, and may bias towards certain aggregation patterns.
evidence: Section 3.3 describes merging single-triple verbalisations: 'the crowd was asked to merge the sentences corresponding to each triple'
Rationale is to 'diminish the risk of having misinterpretations of the original semantics'
Contributors encouraged to 'change the order, and the wording of sentences'
No comparison with direct multi-triple verbalisations
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct human evaluation comparing texts produced by merging vs. direct multi-triple verbalisations. Analyze whether merging produces unnatural transitions or redundancy. Consider collecting some direct multi-triple verbalisations as a control.

comparable_works.relevance: Directly comparable: Wen et al. (2016) created RNNLG, a crowdsourced data-to-text benchmark using enumeration of dialog acts and attribute-value pairs. The present paper explicitly positions itself as addressing limitations of Wen et al. (2016).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: Both use crowdsourcing to create data-to-text corpora. Difference: Wen et al. uses artificial data from hand-written ontologies; present paper uses real RDF data.
